definition: Accelerators will undertake strategic research in their topical areas and, through working with all other Programs, bolster CGIAR’s ability to reach and support targeted end-users while furthering collaboration, coherence, and integration across the entire Portfolio.

The term “Area of Work” is used to refer to the research components of a Program/Accelerator. An Area of Work should be designed as a connected set of activities and outputs which contribute to one or more high-level outputs. An Area of Work may include research activities and/or support activities.

Funding tied to a specific donor or project rather than pooled across the whole portfolio. Window 3 and bilateral results are reported into the Program or Accelerator they are aligned to, alongside that Program's core-funded results.

Activities that develop the know-how and capacity to design, test, validate and use innovations. Examples: training-of-trainers programs at the farmer level; providing guidance on RBM and MEL; training programs with public and private sector partners; educating PhD and MSc students; ongoing institutional support to national partners, particularly NARES; and strengthening government policy analysis.

Non-profit research organizations conducting innovative research. Home to more than 9,000 scientists, researchers, technicians and staff, the Centers work to transform food, land and water systems in a climate crisis.

A request from another Program, Accelerator, or Window 3/Bilateral project asking to link one of your results to theirs as a contributor, or asking you to confirm your own contribution to one of their results. You accept or decline it from Notifications.

HLOs are a means for P/As to plan the topics of work within Areas of Work (AoWs). HLOs are “containers” or “clusters” of work to be delivered on a specific topic or theme. There are multiple HLOs within one AoW. One HLO may contain multiple activities which are thematically aligned but not directly connected (i.e. activities which are led by different groups operating in different locations). HLOs may have indicators defined which are somewhat aggregated and used to track multi-year P/A delivery. For example, an HLO indicator might be “ten innovations to be developed relating to climate information services”. A combination of PODs and window 3 / bilateral projects may contribute to the delivery of these HLO indicators over the years the P/A is active.

Is a standardized measurement that provides evidence or information on progress or change toward achieving specific targets or goals used to trace and compare results, monitor trends, identify areas for action across impact pathways over time and across contexts.

CGIAR Initiatives are the main vehicle for delivery of research and innovation by CGIAR towards 2030. CGIAR's 32 Initiatives are major, prioritized areas of investment that bring capacity from within and without the System to bear on well-defined major problem statements to deliver across five CGIAR Impact Areas. They state quantitatively what impacts and outcomes they intend to achieve, by when, and then work backwards to generate compelling theories of change (TOCs), activities and resource requirements. They come with evaluable results frameworks and clear reporting of results against investment. Initiatives may be targeted at global, regional or country levels.

The process of developing innovations from an idea to a proven product, technology, service or arrangement that is validated for its ability to contribute to positive impacts when used at scale. The process often includes basic research, innovation design, and improving innovations based on testing under (semi-)controlled and uncontrolled conditions. Progress in innovation development is measured in an evidence-based way along the 0-9 levels of innovation readiness. (Scaling Readiness/ IPSR-term: www.scalingreadiness.org).

Combinations of interrelated (bundles of) innovations and enabling conditions that, together, can lead to transformation and impact at scale. Innovation packages are context-, outcome-, and use-group-specific and their ability to contribute to outcomes and impact can change over time. Not to be confused with a Package of deliverables (POD), which is a planning and reporting concept for grouping deliverables. (Scaling Readiness/ IPSR-term: www.scalingreadiness.org; see also: Innovation Bundle).

CGIAR's approach for mainstreaming scaling across the research-to-impact pathway. IPSR embeds scaling as a continuous, stage-gated process — from early characterization of innovations through to sustained use at scale— covering four integrated areas: innovation profiling, innovation packaging, scaling strategies, and innovation portfolio management. Combining innovation readiness with innovation use, it provides the evidence base for decisions on what innovations to advance, adapt, or pause. (Scaling Readiness/ IPSR-term: www.scalingreadiness.org)

A metric used to assess the extent to which an innovation is already being used, by which type of users and under which conditions, with a scale ranging from no use (lowest level - 0) to common use (highest level - 9). An innovation that is only used by the project, design or intervention team or its direct partners will score low in innovation use. Innovations that are commonly used by anticipated end-users will score high in innovation use. Users that are directly incentivized by a project or intervention to use an innovation are considered project team or direct partners which will score as low innovation use. (Scaling Readiness/ IPSR-term: www.scalingreadiness.org).

A specific, measurable target used to track a Program's progress within an Area of Work — for example, a count of results planned for a given topic. The Reporting page shows how many KPIs have been reported against the number planned for each AoW.

Knowledge products are intellectual assets generated from research and development activities such as articles, briefs, reports, extension and training content, databases, software, and multimedia elements that contribute to behavioral changes in particular actors.
A reporting cycle with its own open and close dates — for example, "Reporting 2026 (Open)". Results, requests, and other reporting activity are scoped to whichever phase you have selected.

Policies, strategies, legal instruments, programs, budgets, or investments at different scales (local to global) that have been modified in design or implementation, with evidence that the change was informed by CGIAR research.

The CGIAR System Framework approved by the System’s Funders and Centers in June 2016, and then amended in October 2024, defines “CGIAR Portfolio” as the research programs and/or platforms carried out by the Centers and the CGIAR System Partners in support of the CGIAR Strategy and Results Framework and which are supported by (i) the CGIAR Trust Fund and/or (ii) bilateral sources contractually aligned to such programs and/or platforms.

CGIAR Programs are the main vehicle for delivery of research and innovation by CGIAR from 2025 to 2030. Programs serve as entry points to describe CGIAR’s offer on a key topic, elevating CGIAR’s visibility in global agendas and facilitating the continuation and formation of inclusive alliances and partnerships. They state quantitatively what impacts and outcomes they intend to achieve, along a theory of change. They come with evaluable results frameworks and clear reporting of results against investment. Bilateral and window 3 projects are aligned to Programs and Accelerators and their results are reported as part of Program and Accelerator reporting.
The positive/negative, direct/indirect, and intended/unintended change or consequence of a planned project/program activity or intervention in the form of output, outcome or impact.
The Reporting Tool's on-screen label for a Program (see Program) — the two terms refer to the same entity.

An explicit, testable model of how and why social change is expected to happen along an impact pathway in a development context. A basic research-for-development ToC identifies the context and key actors in a project, program or initiative and specifies the causal pathways and mechanisms by which the research aims to contribute to outcomes and impacts. This model can be used for: (i) designing and planning project logic including assumptions; (ii) monitoring and evaluation of processes and results including risk identification and mitigation; (iii) testing assumptions and identifying lessons learned, reflection for accountability and RBM, and using finding for evidence-based decision making for learning and accountability.

The System's pooled, core funding channels, as distinct from bilateral or Window 3 (W3) funding tied to a specific donor or project. Results are tagged with the funding window they were delivered under.
